    RN-478 — permissions.json lives where the api REACHES, the terminal scope points to the HOST

    The project root had one derivation (projectScopeRoot) and two consumers with opposite needs. That was right while the two modes with a user folder were bind-mount; it stopped being so when runner mode was born (RN-423, ADR 0104), because it's deliberately without bind-mount.

    consumer needs why
    terminal scope (ADR 0055) the host's path that's where the command runs — on the user's machine, through the runner
    permissions.json (the api reads and writes) a path the api reaches it writes it from inside its container

    They're two derivations, and both live in the same file — the source remains single, what split was the question. projectScopeRoot stays unchanged; permissionsFilePath is new and diverges from it at a single point: in runner mode the file goes to <PROJECT_WORKSPACES_ROOT>/<workspace_dir_name>/permissions.json, the managed root, keyed by the name RN-109 freezes at creation. container and mounted don't change — in mounted the folder is a bind-mount, and moving the file would break projects that already have it on disk with no gain.

    Why the managed root and not the user's disk, given the code is there: permissions.json is policy, not project code. Who reads it is the api; the runner never reads it (it receives an already approved command) and the engine doesn't touch it at any point — all mentions of it in apps/engine/lib are comments. Keeping it on the user's machine would make it editable by whoever it restricts, and unreadable precisely when the runner is disconnected, which is when the decision needs to remain valid.

    What this fixed. Execution activation is the first write of the file, and it did mkdir -p of a host path inside the api's container: EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/home/<usuario>' → 500. The read degraded silently (ENOENT → EMPTY_PERMISSIONS_FILE), and that's why the bigger effect slipped through unseen: in a runner project the permissions.json never existed, and decide() always fell to require_approval because of a file that wasn't there.

    Declared cost: for a runner project, the policy file no longer lives next to the code — whoever looks for it in the project folder won't find it.

    A typed refusal, and 400 instead of 500. The derivation's two throw new Error(...) become LocalizacaoDeProjetoInvalidaError, in the mold of CaminhoLocalInvalidoError: a readable motivo in pt-BR, and ActivateExecutionUseCase maps it to 400. An incoherent project row (the (mode, path) pair only becomes invalid by being written outside creation) now says what to fix instead of becoming a body-less 500. The Overview screen now shows that message — it printed the constant "Could not activate execution" while the twin button in the session chat already used mensagemDaApi: same button, two diagnoses.

    The gap that REMAINS, declared: the engine has the same defect and it wasn't fixed here. Engine.Actions.Workspace.ensure!/4 does File.mkdir_p!(workspace_dir(project_id)), which in a runner project is the host's path — the dev agent's working tree has nowhere to be born. It doesn't become a 500 (the rescue of ensure_remoto/2 returns {:error, …}), it becomes a dev agent that doesn't work. Fixing it in isolation would be materializing a worktree on the host through a path that container execution replaces; what changes now is only the message, which names the cause instead of passing on a raw "permission denied".

    • Test: apps/api/test/infrastructure/filesystem/project-workspaces-root.spec.ts (permissionsFilePath in the three modes; and the non-regression of projectScopeRoot still returning the host's path in runner/mounted — unifying the two back would break ADR 0055), apps/api/test/application/use-cases/execution/activate-execution.use-case.spec.ts (with the REAL FsPermissionsFileStore: the file lands in the managed root and the host folder stays untouched; an incoherent row becomes a 400 that teaches), apps/web/src/routes/ProjectOverviewTab.test.tsx (the api's message on screen), apps/engine/test/engine/actions/workspace_runner_test.exs (the failure names the cause in a runner project, and passes intact in the other modes)

    RN-479 — Every hybrid search writes a row in rag_searches, with FROZEN weights; and telemetry never takes down the search

    apps/api/src/domain/rag/rag-search-limits.ts declares, in its own comment, that none of the four hybrid search numbers (the two weights, the threshold, and the number of candidates) comes from calibration with real data. It didn't because there was no way to: the search left no trace at all — neither a table row nor an event. Calibrating without measuring would be trading one guess for another.

    HybridSearchUseCase now writes, on each search, what it returned (hits, with the 1-based rank of each excerpt), under which conditions (degraded/vector_available), how long it took (latency_ms), who searched (actor_kind/actor_id), and in which session — or in NONE.

    Why a TABLE and not just a session event. session_events.session_id is NOT NULL, and a search coming from the RAG tab is a PROJECT one: it has no session. Recording it only as an event would lose exactly the searches in which a human looked at the scores and judged, which are the ones carrying the real signal. It's the same class of problem that forced the embedding metering cut (ADR 0075, token_usage.session_id NOT NULL), and the way out is the same: an own table, with NULLABLE session_id.

    pesos frozen in the row is the point. pesosVigentes() copies the values of the moment into the record — the same discipline as the frozen price in metering (ADR 0042) and the image_version in project_containers. Without the copy, the first calibration that touched RAG_SEARCH_WEIGHT_VECTOR would make all the previous measurement start meaning something else, silently — and "did it improve after the change?", the only question telemetry exists to answer, would become impossible to ask.

    Recording telemetry NEVER takes down the search, and also doesn't fail SILENTLY. Whoever asks shouldn't lose the answer because the measuring instrument went down; and the repository is explicit about failure that becomes silence (RN-059). So a failing INSERT becomes a log with the origin classified (infra, RN-023) and searchId: null in the response — which isn't the same as "there was no result": it's "there's nothing to attach a vote to", and the screen needs both separate so as not to offer a control the api would refuse (RN-088).

    degraded and vector_available are two columns on purpose, and today's redundancy (degraded = !vector_available) is declared in the schema instead of hidden: vector_available is a fact about the PROVIDER — it's what makes medir:rag fail —, and degraded is the word of the CONTRACT with the engine, whose definition may grow.

    RN-480 — The vote on an excerpt is the only TRUTH signal of the measurement, and it requires the reference the search returned

    Latency and degradation rate say whether the search RAN; only the vote says whether it GOT IT RIGHT. rag_feedback keeps that vote — two values (util/irrelevante) and not a 1-to-5 scale, because a fine scale invites differences of ruler between voters that no aggregation recovers later.

A searchId that doesn't exist in that project, and a chunkId that wasn't among the hits of that search, are refused before any write. It isn't decorative rigor: the rank of the voted excerpt is what separates two diagnoses that precision@1 confuses — a poor index doesn't return the right excerpt in any position, a wrong weight returns the right excerpt at rank 7. A vote without rank produces a meaningless number, which is worse than no number.

    The refusal applies on both paths: through the tab it becomes a 400 on screen; through the agent it becomes an error tool-result the model can fix in the next iteration (RN-061/RN-163), never a crash.

    One vote per actor per excerpt per search (unique (search_id, chunk_id, actor_id), with onConflictDoUpdate): changing one's mind overwrites one's own vote. Without the lock, whoever clicked twice would weigh double in precision@k and the metric would start measuring enthusiasm.

    The role is viewer, the SAME as search — whoever can read the result is whoever can judge it (RN-102: the minimum is the endpoint's, and voting neither spends nor configures anything). The agent's tool is :direct, never proposed_action: grading an excerpt isn't an external effect, and turning it into an action to approve would fill the queue with noise.

    RN-486 — REGISTERED state and OBSERVED state never merge, and "didn't look" has its own reason

    project_containers keeps what was REGISTERED. The daemon answers what is OBSERVED. Before the broker the table had no way to lie (container_id was always NULL); now it has, and the read says so instead of hiding it.

    The lifecycle route returns both, separately. A container killed from outside appears as registered running and observed exited, and that's how it has to appear. The reconciliation is ON READ, not a background daemon.

It means two different things, and naoObservado is what separates them: null there means the observation HAPPENED and came back empty — the positive statement "I looked and there's no container" —, while broker-nao-configurado, broker-sem-resposta, and broker-recusou mean it wasn't possible to look, each with a different fix.     No broker refusal takes down the read. The registered lifecycle is legitimate information on its own and existed before the broker; losing it because the broker is down would trade data we have for data we don't.

    Declared gap: an orphan container of a project that never had a lifecycle row doesn't appear on that route — it reads the registered first. What finds orphans is the sweep by brabo.managed=true, and the page that consumes it doesn't exist yet.

    RN-490 — The RAG accuracy golden-set measures by FILE PATH, in the TOP-5, never by exact chunk or rank 1

    The rag-acertivo gate (docs/gates.yml) measures whether the hybrid search returns the right file for 17 questions composed from real RNs/ADRs of this repository (golden-set, ADR 0123's mold applied to RAG).     RN-493 — A terminal inside the real container gains an auto-approval FLOOR, without touching the absolute ceilings

    The justification is a SECOND boundary, not the absence of the first. The lexical terminal scope (terminalNoEscopo, ADR 0055) keeps running over the SAME HOST paths as always — the cwd/command arriving at decide() are NEVER translated to /work (that translation only happens later, in the engine — RN-492). Inside the real container, a STRONGER boundary is added on top of the lexical one: Docker's mount namespace, which the process physically doesn't cross, plus the /work validation the broker already does (DiretorioForaDoEscopoError). It's defense in depth — the lexical scope isn't replaced, it's redundant.

On the web, ApprovalCard.podeSemprePermitir hides the "always allow" button for container_remove, the same ruler that already applies to instruction_patch.

    ContainerBrokerPort.remove is docker rm --force — it removes even a running container, in a single call. The state machine has NO direct running -> removed (only running -> stopped/failed, and only FROM THERE to removed): ExecuteContainerRemoveUseCase registers BOTH hops when the registered state still said running (stopped, then removed), reflecting what really happened on the Docker side without widening the state machine with a shortcut that would only exist here.

    Neither of the two decides an image — unlike container_start, which reuses DecidirImagemDoProjetoUseCase to emit a new version of artifact.project_image. stop/remove only ask the broker to act on the container that already exists.

    The single base of mounted projects (RN-500)

    RN-500 — There's ONE base for mounted projects, it's mounted by identity, and absent means "don't offer the mode"

    BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE is the only folder of the operator's computer that Brabo's containers see. It's mounted by identity ($X:$X) in the api and engine services, which means the path is the SAME on the host and inside both containers.

    The identity isn't a style preference. The projects.workspace_path string is typed by the user and shown back to them; with host ≠ container the product would have to choose which of the two to keep, and any choice makes the screen lie to someone. And it's what makes projectScopeRoot (api) and Engine.Actions.Workspace.workspace_dir/2 (engine) remain correct without a single new line of code — the leading-slash discriminator still holds, and the terminal scope of ADR 0055 keeps authorizing exactly the folder the user sees.

    Absent is a NORMAL state, not an error. baseDeProjetos() returns null when the variable isn't defined or is empty, and NEVER throws. null travels to the client through GET /workspaces/:workspaceId/projects-base (maintainer, the same minimum as POST .../projects, because it's to decide what that route offers that the value exists) and that's how project creation learns not to offer the Mounted folder mode. Offering a mode the installation doesn't honor produces a project that locks up later, at the first tool of the first agent, far from the screen where the decision was made — it's the same lesson as RN-170.

    dentroDaBaseDeProjetos reuses dentroDoEscopo, the same function as the terminal scope, and not a prefix comparison written again: the trap is exactly the one it already solves — /home/voce/brabo2 is not inside /home/voce/brabo, although the string starts the same. The base itself counts as inside; with a null base, nothing is inside.

    The base is its OWN variable, never PROJECT_WORKSPACES_HOST_DIR. The three reasons are in the ADR, and the first has data consequences: a managed workspace is named by workspace_dir_name (UNIQUE) and a mounted project is named by the user, so <base>/loja and a container project with workspace_dir_name = loja would land in the SAME physical folder, with init_from_bare! doing git init inside the other's project.

    The checkout guard lives in the preflight, and it's the only place where it's possible. pnpm dev refuses to come up when the base overlaps Brabo's checkout, in both directions. The api can't do that check: it compares against process.cwd(), which inside its container is /workspace, and never sees the real path on disk. Without that guard, whoever clones Brabo into $HOME/brabo and points the base there passes all the existing validation and makes the dev agents execute inside the product's own tree — ADR 0055's failure coming in through a door it doesn't watch.

    What this RN does NOT do: it doesn't require a mounted project to be inside the base. caminhoDeWorkspaceLocalValido and projectScopeRoot stay intact — that predicate runs on every READ, and a legacy mounted project outside the base would start blowing up when read. The base is a CREATION and CONVERSION rule, and comes in the next RN.

    The mounted folder is born when the container comes up (RN-501)

    RN-501 — mounted validates only the LEXICON and the base at creation; the folder is MATERIALIZED later, by whoever has authority over the disk

    Creating a mounted project stopped touching disk. It requires two things, and both are lexical:

    1. the same predicate runner already used (caminhoDeWorkspaceLocalValido) — absolute, no .., outside the root and system folders, not overlapping Brabo's checkout (RN-422/RN-423);
    2. being inside BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE (RN-500), which is the only folder of the computer the api's and the engine's containers see.

    The project is born with workspaceVerifiedAt: null, exactly like a runner.

    Why postpone. The requirement is the product owner's and it's literal: "if it's a Mounted folder, the bind-mount must be created AFTER the architect's decision". Disk validation ran at CREATION, which is the first screen of the flow, and the Arquiteto's decision happens many sessions later — requiring the folder ready at creation is requiring it before any decision exists. And it's what prevented mounted from being a first-class choice: a path SUGGESTED by the wizard (<base>/<slug>) is, by construction, a path that doesn't exist yet.

    The difference between mounted and runner was never what counts as a valid path — it's when and who confirms the disk. In runner it's the CLI connecting; in mounted it's the materialization.

    Without a configured base, the MODE isn't available. The refusal says so, with the variable's name and what the operator needs to do — it never pretends the path was what was wrong. Outside the base, the refusal names the base and suggests <base>/<the name the person asked for>, never the bare base, which would teach putting the project at the root of all of them. Both messages come from ONE source (motivoDeForaDaBaseDeProjetos), because the two doors that apply the rule — creation/conversion and materialization — refuse for the same reason.

    The materialization (materializarWorkspaceMontado) is mkdir -p plus the usual three disk questions (does it exist? is it a folder? can it be written?), with the refusal for being outside the base before the mkdir — otherwise a path written outside the product would make the api create a folder anywhere it reaches. Two callers:

    • ExecuteContainerStartUseCase — the normal one. When the Infra brings up the container, the folder is created, proven writable, and workspace_verified_at is stamped by the SAME path ConfirmProjectWorkspaceUseCase uses. Failing is a NAMED failed, never a throw nor a 500 — the same discipline as BrokerIndisponivelError/RunnerNaoConectadoError —, and the lifecycle does not get marked provisioning: marking it and only then finding out that it can't write would leave project_containers asserting a state that never existed. The message names the variable, the path, the probable cause (the folder's owner on the host; the images run non-root, ADR 0024), and the next step ("approve container_start again").
    • ConvertProjectExecutionModeUseCase — the exception, declared. Conversion has no container step to hang the work on, and right after it MOVES permissions.json to permissionsFilePath(localNova), which in mounted is the user's folder. Moving a file into a nonexistent folder fails, so here mkdir-at-decision is right — before the transaction, so the refusal doesn't leave a transaction open, and becoming a 400.

    What this RN does NOT do, and it's the easiest regression to cause. The base rule does not go into caminhoDeWorkspaceLocalValido. That predicate runs on EVERY READ, through projectScopeRoot (terminal scope, permissions.json, Code tab), and a LEGACY mounted project — created when the bind-mount was one compose line per project, therefore outside the base — would start blowing up with LocalizacaoDeProjetoInvalidaError when simply read. The base is a creation and conversion rule; the lexicon is forever.

    No migration, and the database CHECK stays intact. mounted keeps writing a NON-null workspace_path, so (execution_mode <> 'container') = (workspace_path IS NOT NULL) remains satisfied. Postponing verification never touches the pairing invariant.

    Declared consequence: between creating the project and bringing up the container, workspace_path points to a folder that may not exist. Nothing breaks (projectScopeRoot is lexical; permissions.json degrades to EMPTY_PERMISSIONS_FILE, which is require_approval on everything), but the screen needs to SAY so — a screen that shows a path without saying it doesn't exist yet is a screen asserting what it doesn't know.

    A mounted project brings up a container through the BROKER (RN-503)

    RN-503 — A mounted project brings up a container through the BROKER, and what crosses the network is a discriminated locator — never an absolute path

    A project in Mounted folder mode couldn't get any container until now, and for two independent blocks: ExecuteContainerStartUseCase sent every mode other than container to the RUNNER (which requires a connected brabo-runner), and the broker refused at the source any mode that wasn't container, with ModoDeExecucaoNaoSuportadoError.

    Both existed for the same reason of GEOMETRY, not because of the mode's name: the folder of a mounted project was in an arbitrary place on the operator's disk, which the server's Docker daemon had no reason to see. ADR 0141 (RN-500) changed that geometry — every mounted project now lives under one base mounted by identity —, and that's what, and only what, this rule harvests.

    The branching is now by DESTINATION, not by mode. container and mounted go to the BROKER; only runner goes to the runner, because its folder remains on a machine this server doesn't reach (ADR 0137). The same holds for the three lifecycle actions — container_start, container_stop, and container_remove: they HAVE to change together, otherwise a mounted project's container comes up on the server and the request to stop goes looking for it on the user's machine, leaving up, with no way to stop it, what is up.

    ADR 0130's invariant doesn't move: no absolute path crosses the network. The broker is root-equivalent on the host and COMPOSES the -v from ITS roots; if the api sent /home/voce/brabo/loja, the bind-mount's containment would come to depend on the api being correct, which is exactly the dependency the broker exists not to have. What changes is that now there are TWO roots on the other side, so the spec needs to SAY against which of them the relative piece applies — and it says so, in a discriminated locator:

    localizacao.tipo segment broker root
    gerenciada workspace_dir_name (RN-109) PROJECT_WORKSPACES_HOST_ROOT
    montada the RELATIVE path under the base BRABO_PROJECTS_HOST_BASE
    indisponivel — (there's a motivo) none

    Three states and not two, because the third really exists and has two different fixes: a runner project (the folder is on another machine — the fix is the runner, on the other side) and a LEGACY mounted project created outside the base (the fix is moving the folder). Collapsing them into a null would make the same absence send whoever operates to the wrong place. The folder that IS the base itself also falls here, and doesn't become an empty segment: <raiz>/ would mount the whole base — the folder of ALL mounted projects — inside the container of a single one.

    The lack of one root is never supplied by the other. Without BRABO_PROJECTS_HOST_BASE, a mounted project's start refuses naming the variable (BaseDeProjetosNaoConfiguradaError, origin infra, 503) and doesn't touch any container — the same mold as RaizDeWorkspacesNaoConfiguradaError. Falling to the other root by omission would be the worst possible outcome: the managed root is named by workspace_dir_name and the base is named by the user, so the same name points to different folders and the container would come up with ANOTHER project's folder, with nothing indicating why. For the same reason, the list of modes the broker serves is an ALLOWLIST: a new mode in the enum is born refused, with a message, instead of accepted by omission.

    The composition still goes through three barriers, not one. The api refuses what isn't under the base (segmentoSobABaseDeProjetos); the broker refuses a segment that isn't relative (segmentoDeProjetoValidado — .., absolute, empty, double slash, NUL); and the concatenation's result still goes through raizDeProjetoValidada before becoming a -v. Validating the segment and not validating the concatenation would be trusting string arithmetic.

    mounted ELECTS the image, like container — it doesn't read the current one like the runner. It isn't aesthetic symmetry: it's the only design that works. The broker composes from artifact.project_image, going to FETCH it from the api. An Infra election that wasn't recorded in that artifact would be inert — the container would come up with the image the Arquiteto decided, the payload the human approved would say another, and nothing in the record would expose the difference. The runner's path can read the current one precisely because there the api SENDS the spec's fields through the channel; there the artifact isn't the source the other side consults.

    What this rule does NOT do: it materializes no folder — whoever creates the folder of the mounted project is RN-501, in the SAME use case and before this branching, precisely because the server's daemon needs the folder to exist to mount it. It also doesn't touch the image gate (RN-105 already applies to the three modes since RN-494) and doesn't change who PROPOSES container_start — the Infra Lead can still propose for a project with no connected runner and no decided image, the gap declared since RN-494.

    The conversational agents' decision artifact (RN-505)

    RN-508 — container_start_via_runner: a second action type to bring up the container, exclusive to runner, and the Infra Lead refuses blind proposals BEFORE proposing

    container_start (ADR 0130/0133) requires imagem/network/resources/ rationale — the Infra ELECTS a candidate from the Arquiteto's routing. Until this delivery, the same action type also served execution_mode: runner (ExecuteContainerStartUseCase.executeViaRunner), but the runner's path NEVER read any of those four fields: the image that comes up is the one already DECIDED (there's no routing to elect against, because the broker never reaches a runner project's folder). Asking for 4 fields the dispatch always discarded is the defect that motivates a separate ACTION being born instead of a "smart" container_start branching by mode.

    container_start_via_runner only has rationale (optional). The same caliber as container_start (maintainer, require_approval by default, never seeded in auto-approval, configurable in permissions.json like the other three container actions — it doesn't enter the absolute ceiling of container_remove). ExecuteContainerStartUseCase loses the whole runner branch (executeViaRunner, ApiToEngineClient/ObterSpecDeContainerUseCase leave the constructor) — it becomes exclusive to container/mounted, both through the BROKER (RN-503). The extracted code becomes ExecuteContainerStartViaRunnerUseCase, a sibling file. The lifecycle dance (provisioning -> running) the two paths shared by copy becomes SubirCicloDeVidaDoContainerUseCase (apps/api/.../containers/) — extracted so as not to duplicate the state machine's rationale in the two files.

    The Infra Lead queries LOCALLY, without HTTP, before proposing. The new tool (Engine.Infra.Tools.ProposeContainerStartViaRunner) is intercepted by Engine.Infra.InfraLeadServer.dispatch_calls/2, which reads Project.get/1 (execution_mode) and Engine.Runners.Registry.connected?/1 (runner connected) — BOTH reads are already local, in the same BEAM process — BEFORE calling propose_action. It refuses with a NAMED reason (never proposes blindly) when the project is in container (use propose_container_start), in mounted (likewise, since RN-503), or in runner with no runner connected now. This gap — "proposing without knowing whether it'll work" — is the SAME one propose_container_start has had since RN-494, declared and accepted for that tool (touching the Infra Lead's prompt/instruction would be outside the API/domain scope); the NEW tool is born without it, because it's born knowing how to refuse.

    The specification the api composes is the one the runner VALIDATES, and that is now proven. EspecificacaoDeContainerParaRunner is the fields of EntradaDeEspecificacao (packages/docker-port) minus raizDoProjeto, which only the runner knows — TEN, not nine. It was born with nine, without projectId, and the consequence was that this path NEVER brought up any container since it existed: the engine passes the map on opaquely, the runner hands it to especificacaoValidada, which requires projectId as non-empty text, and the action ended failed with "especificação de container recusada em projectId: esperava texto não vazio, recebi undefined" — and from there the CORRECT block of RN-507/RN-502 did the rest, with no dev agent claiming a task. The data always existed (SpecDeContainer.projectId, the same one the BROKER receives through GET .../container-spec, and that's why only runner mode broke); it just wasn't copied. Three green suites didn't catch it because each one built its own fixture: the use case's test asserted what it itself expected, the runner's built a fixture WITH projectId, and the engine doesn't look at the map. What is now guaranteed is the CHAIN — the payload ExecuteContainerStartViaRunnerUseCase composes, going through the real especificacaoValidada —, and the test also locks the set of fields: raizDoProjeto is the only one the api doesn't send, so a new field on one side without the other fails.

    The folder browser served by the api (RN-504)

    RN-509 — A module Dev Agent's "Always allow" scopes to agent_autonomy, PER AGENT — no longer the whole project's permissions.json

    ApproveAlwaysActionUseCase always wrote to permissions.json/allow — WHOLE PROJECT scope, shared by any actor. That meant "always allowing" a command for dev-checkout released the SAME command for dev-auth, for dev-lead, and for any future agent of the project: the intent of whoever clicked ("I trust THIS agent with THIS") had no way to be expressed — only "I trust anyone with this" existed.

    The write now branches by ACTOR, inside the SAME use case (not a new one — duplicating the two absolute-ceiling guards for out-of-scope terminal/git_push/sudo and for container_remove in two places would be the same defect RN-418/RN-495 already exist to avoid):

    • An agent actor whose id is dev-<modulo> (ADR 0053/PHASE 14d — the DYNAMIC dev area, one agent per module_map module): writes to agent_autonomy(projectId, agentId, actionType) = auto_approve, through the SAME AgentAutonomyRepository.upsert that activate-execution.use-case.ts already calls to seed the three git actions per module. permissions.json stays untouched.
    • Any other actor — user, system, an agent agent that isn't a module dev, and dev-lead — keeps going to the usual permissions.json/allow, whole-project scope, exactly as before.

    dev-lead is the exception that needs its own name. ehDevDeModulo (agent-areas.ts) is PURE agentId.startsWith('dev-'), on purpose — and that classifies dev-lead as true. What excludes the lead from its own area is ehMembroDe, not ehDevDeModulo alone ("the lead isn't a member of its own area" holds for any area — duplicating the exclusion inside the predicate left both copies unreachable by tests, a finding recorded in the comment of agent-areas.ts itself). That's why the branch uses ehDevDeModulo(actor.id) && actor.id !== DEV_LEAD: without the second term, "always allow" clicked on a dev-lead action would write module autonomy under the LEAD's agentId by accident — an agent that isn't a member of dev, has no module, and that the area never looks at via agent_area_members.

    The two absolute ceilings of decide.ts keep running BEFORE the branch, without changing order. Terminal with a git external effect (git push, gh pr create) or privileged (sudo/doas) — RN-106/RN-418 — and container_remove — RN-495 — keep refusing the WHOLE click (400, the action not even approved), for ANY actor, before the project is even fetched. Scoping the write per agent isn't a second door to the same ceiling: the two refusal ifs stay where they were, and the new branch comes after.

    The permission.granted event carries one payload OR the other, never one pretending to be the other. { pattern } remains the format of the permissions.json path (the text pattern written to the file); the new path emits { agentId, actionType } — there's no "pattern" at all to show when the write is a table row keyed by agent.

    No data migration. Old "always allow" entries written for a module dev in permissions.json, from before this rule existed, stay there exactly as they were — they just no longer receive MORE entries of that kind from then on. A conscious decision by the product owner, not a forgotten gap.

    The mirror destination is per project (RN-515)

    RN-515 — The mirror destination is declared PER PROJECT and is never global; null is the normal state; and the api validates ONLY the lexicon, saying it is only the lexicon

    The espelho capability (RN-514, ADR 0147) copies the agents' work to a user folder outside the mounted base — which is the reason it exists, because a bind mount does not cross a network nor reach a path outside what was mounted. This rule decides where that destination lives and how the user declares it; it does not copy any file.

    PER PROJECT, never global. The destination is the projects.mirror_path column and the project's mirrorPath field, written by PUT /projects/:projectId/mirror-path (maintainer, the same minimum as execution-mode and projects-base: the route speaks of a path on the operator's computer). Never a global setting in the runner, never an environment variable: a global destination would make project B's artifact land in project A's folder, and the user would find that out through the content, not through an error (ADR 0147, point 4).

    null is the NORMAL state, not a pending item. The column is nullable and is born null; a project without a mirror is the majority, and the product never picks a destination on its own. Clearing is {"mirrorPath": null} — the key is mandatory, and omitting it is 400: a body that omits the field would be indistinguishable from "clear", and clearing silently is precisely the defect. Clearing always works, even in a container project, otherwise a converted row would be stuck in the state the rule forbids.

    Only the LEXICON, and the api SAYS it is only the lexicon. The api does not see the machine where the destination will exist — it is the situation of the runner mode (RN-423), not that of mounted, where the folder ends up inside the base the api actually reaches. It reuses caminhoDeWorkspaceLocalValido, the same predicate as creation and conversion (absolute, no ../., never the root nor a system folder, never overlapping the Brabo checkout), instead of a fourth copy of the same rule — and it does not require BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE, because the mirror destination is by definition the folder the base does not cover. The refusal message declares that the disk was not verified and who verifies it.

    The two directions of the same loop. A destination inside the workspacePath and a destination that contains the workspacePath are the same refusal seen from two sides (ADR 0147, point 2): writing the mirror inside the source makes the mirror copy itself, and a source inside the destination nests the copy on every round. Refusing one and allowing the other would be closing the door and leaving the window open. The comparison is by SEGMENT (dentroDoEscopo), never raw startsWith: /base-outra is not inside /base, and refusing it would penalize a perfectly legitimate sibling folder.

    This is the LEXICAL half of the guard, and only it. The other is realpath, and it belongs to the RUNNER (espelho-guard.ts, ADR 0147 point 2), on the machine where both paths really exist. A symlink in any segment of the destination pointing back to the source passes through here unseen — the api has no disk on which to resolve it. The api did not guarantee the loop; it prevented the WRITTEN loop.

    container is refused, and the refusal is NAMED. The source of a container project is a managed volume on the server, and whoever would copy is a process on the user's machine, which does not see it. Accepting and never copying would be worse than refusing, because it would look configured. mounted and runner can. For the same reason, converting the mode ZEROES the destination (RN-447..450): in container it could not exist, and even between mounted and runner the conversion MOVES the source against which both directions of the loop were validated.

    The value comes back in every project read (ProjectResponseDto.mirrorPath), so the mirror implementation and the status screen do not need a new route. There is no dedicated read endpoint.

    And it is NOT a proposed_action. Writing the mirror is configuration the user declared, not an agent asking to act — ADR 0147 is explicit about it, and syncing via a terminal command would fall into the scope of ADR 0055 and become a queue of routine approvals.

    The mirror state is visible, and the three states do not collapse (RN-517)

    RN-517 — The outcome of each mirror round comes back through the channel and becomes TELEMETRY in its own table; "never synced", "synced and copied nothing" and "failed" are THREE answers, and success and error coexist

    Session 8 of PHASE 28 and point 7 of ADR 0147. RN-516 made the mirror really copy and left mirror_sync fire-and-forget — with no mirror_sync_result in the protocol, on purpose, because the telemetry format was this delivery's decision. It is this one that closes the loop.

    The path is that of workspace_confirm, and no other. The runner pushes mirror_sync_result on the terminal:<projectId> channel after the round ends; the engine handles it in handle_in/3 and RELAYS it to the api over internal HTTP (POST /internal/projects/:projectId/mirror-sync-result), which writes through the use case. The engine does not write the table — a second write path would be the second source of the same truth, and the first thing to diverge. It is the only precedent of the runner telling something about itself, and that is why the ADR named it.

    Never an optimistic "ok". The reported outcome is the REAL one: the three counts that sincronizarEspelho returned (copied, skipped, refused — never recounted) or the named error. ALL THREE exits of tratarMirrorSync report, and with different messages: the refusal for a non-granted destination, the copy failure and the success. ok is NEVER deduced from there being a count or a message — neither in the runner, nor in the engine's translation, nor in the api's use case: deducing would make a round that copied 0 files (perfectly normal) indistinguishable from one that never even ran.

    A TABLE, and not the event log. project_mirror_states, one row per project (unique project_id, same design as project_containers). The reason is the same one that made rag_searches become a table (RN-479): session_events.session_id is NOT NULL and a mirror round has no session — the event log would lose the whole thing, not part of it. And it is not a proposed_action under any circumstances: writing the mirror is configuration the user declared, not an agent asking to act.

    The THREE states of RN-088, and they do not collapse. "Never synced" is the absent row. "Synced and copied nothing" is a present row with files_copied = 0 — an outcome, not an emptiness. "Failed" is last_error_at more recent than last_synced_at. They are three different answers, the person acts differently on each one, and a dash serving all three would be the screen refusing to name what it knows (RN-470).

    Success and error COEXIST in the same row. The two writes mention disjoint columns: the success one does not touch last_error/last_error_at, the failure one does not touch any success column, and neither erases the other. What decides which one is CURRENT is the comparison of the two timestamps (deriveMirrorSyncStatus, a pure domain function), and that is what lets the screen say "the last round failed — last good copy yesterday, with 412 files". A destructive write of one side over the other would throw away precisely the most useful information the screen has while the mirror is broken. Two smaller choices in the same direction: a failure WITHOUT a destination does not erase the destination of the last copy that worked, and an exact timestamp tie resolves to failed — between asserting that everything is fine and asserting that something failed, the safe assertion is the one that makes the person look.

    destination is FROZEN, like image_version in project_containers and the weights in rag_searches (RN-479): it is the REAL destination of that round, resolved by realpath on the user's machine after the mkdir -p. Reading projects.mirror_path at display time would state the destination of NOW over a copy from yesterday — and the two really diverge, because the grant travels in the join and only changes when the runner reconnects (RN-516). When they diverge, the screen SAYS so.

    Writing telemetry never takes down what it measures. The copy has already finished when the report goes out; the engine's handle_in only LOGS the api's refusal and returns {:noreply, socket} in both branches, and the runner's channel stays alive. Without a channel (the connection dropped between the request and the end of the copy) the runner does not report and does not throw — the round that happened is not undone because of that. And a project whose destination was CLEARED midway still records: the round happened, and its error is what usually explains what happened.

    On the screen, the row goes into AmbienteDoProjeto (the side column of the Overview, next to those of execution mode and runner) and only exists in a project that has mirrorPath — in a project without a mirror, "never synced" would be an invented absence, the same argument that already held for the runner row. An ABSOLUTE date with a caveat and never a green "it's up" dot, by the same precedent as workspaceVerifiedAt: the timestamp says a round happened, not that the folder is up to date with what changed afterwards (the trigger is a named moment, the commit — never a watcher). The status arrives RESOLVED from the api: the rule deciding which timestamp counts has a single source, and it is what decides which of the three sentences the person reads.

    viewer role to READ, maintainer to write the destination — the rule of RN-102 applied: the minimum belongs to the ENDPOINT, and this one only reads. The destination already travels in every project read (GET /projects/:projectId, viewer), so requiring maintainer here would lock information away from whoever already sees it in the same project, which is the worse of the two defects because it is invisible to whoever lost the capability.

    Revised by RN-685 (ADR 0201): the socket ticket now stores WHICH credential requested it, and revoking a key (and a PAT) takes down only the connections opened WITH IT — another runner of the same user, with another key or with a PAT, stays up. The "declared cost" below no longer holds. The {projeto, usuário} pair survives as the target of member removal (RN-615), as that of the LEGACY connection (ticket without a credential) during the rollout, and as plan B when the engine does not know the per-credential route.

    The one that sends the command is the api; the one that reaches the pid is the engine. The api calls POST /internal/projects/:projectId/runner/disconnect (the same internal HTTP with the usual service token, never a second mechanism), and the engine finds the channel via Engine.Runners.Registry.whereis/1 — the pid it already handed out. The engine does not query the keys table and the api does not talk to the channel; neither of the two does the other's work, the same division as EngineWeb.ContainerCommandController (RN-497).

    The precision that exists is {projeto, usuário}, and the one that does not exist is {chave} — by construction, not by taste. Engine.Runners.SocketTicket stores project_id, user_id and kind, and only that; the api requests the ticket with {userId, kind}. The identity of the CREDENTIAL that originated the ticket (the PAT, or the kid of the device key — RN-475) dies in PatAuthGuard and never reaches the socket. Carrying it there would require a new column in runner_socket_tickets, a new field in the internal request and a new assign in connect/3: an auth contract change, outside this delivery.

    A DECLARED cost, and named in the code, not only here: a runner of the SAME user connected with a PAT, or with another key of the same project, also drops. It reconnects on its own — the next round requests a new ticket, and the credential that is still valid gets one. Whoever was revoked does not, and that is where the revocation bites. A runner of ANOTHER user on the same project does not drop: the comparison is socket.assigns.user_id, inside the channel process, which is the only one that can read it — and the de_outro_dono outcome goes back to the requester instead of an :ok that does not describe what happened.

    It takes down the TRANSPORT, not just the channel process. Stopping only the channel would leave the socket alive and the Phoenix client re-entering the topic forever with an already consumed ticket — silent degradation, exactly the defect ADR 0147 exists not to repeat. EngineWeb.RunnerSocket.id/1 stops being nil and now names the connection (runner_socket:<kind>:<projectId>:<userId>), and the channel uses Phoenix's documented mechanism, Endpoint.broadcast(id, "disconnect", %{}). It is through it that the runner NOTICES the drop: onDisconnected resolves the round, the loop requests a new ticket and the api refuses.

    A side effect NEVER takes down the main effect. The DELETE stays 204 and idempotent: engine down, no runner connected or a timeout cannot make the revocation fail nor become 5xx. The call to the engine lives in a try/catch that only LOGS, inside the use case — the SAME rule as rag_searches (RN-479) and mirror_sync_result (RN-517). And the four outcomes are information, not error: sem_runner is the normal case of whoever revokes an orphan key (RN-519), and an UNKNOWN outcome coming from the engine becomes timeout and never derrubado — between asserting that the connection dropped and asserting that maybe not, the safe assertion is the one that does not promise what is not known.

    Revoke FIRST, take down afterwards, and the project comes from the revoked ROW, never from the URL: the route's projectId was already ignored in the DELETE, and reading it here would make a divergent projectId take down the runner of a project that has nothing to do with this key.

    RN-521 — The /containers page lists EVERY project of the workspace and becomes the HUMAN path to start the container, branched by execution_mode

    Extended by RN-574 (ADR 0161): a fourth local refusal reason, sem_broker_na_instalacao, for container/mounted in an installation without a container broker — after "already up" and before "no image decided".

    Extended by RN-590 (AT-105): the same reading holds in the mode conversion, in stop/remove and in the Infra Lead's proposal (409 refusal from the api when proposing).

    Starting a project's container had one path: the Infra Lead, inside a session, calling its tool. In a real execution of exp004 (runner mode) container_start_via_runner failed due to the defect that RN-508 closed — and there was no way to TRY AGAIN. Five dev agents spent hours emitting dev.blocked_by_container (RN-502), and the only way out was to open a new session and talk to an agent to re-execute a machine operation.

    The global containers page (ADR 0136, RN-495) was already the place where a HUMAN decides a container's lifecycle — but it did not even show the project: the rule was "one row per project that already has project_containers", and a start that fails BEFORE recording leaves no row at all. The screen hid exactly the project for which it needed to exist.

    The THIRD state has its own name, and it is not stopped. The read model becomes a LEFT JOIN (it was INNER) and registrado becomes null for those that never provisioned — it is not a new value of ContainerLifecycleStatus (stopped is a container that EXISTED and stopped), and it is not "not observed" (which is about the daemon having been asked). The screen prints "never provisioned" and the Observed column says sem_container_registrado, the third reason of naoVerificado — the three do not collapse (RN-088/RN-486).

    The list widened; the BUDGET did not. Asking the broker for the observed state is a network call per project, with a ceiling of 20 per load (TETO_DE_VERIFICACOES_POR_CARGA). A project without project_containers has nothing to observe, so it is never eligible and never takes up a slot: in a workspace with hundreds of empty projects, those with a real container stay verified exactly as before. And it remains THREE batch queries, however many projects there are — none inside a loop.

    The action branches by execution_mode, with the same rule as the backend (RN-497/RN-503): container and mounted propose container_start (broker, on the server) and runner proposes container_start_via_runner (local agent, on the user's machine). The TWO payloads are different on purpose and are not copied: container_start carries the image ELECTION (image, network, resources), read from the project's current decision at click time; container_start_via_runner has a schema with only rationale (RN-508), because it starts the ALREADY decided image and elects nothing.

    The screen does NOT propose what is already known to fail — and says the reason in place of the button. Three refusals, each with its own text, in the order "state of the WORLD before the capability of whoever is looking" (so a viewer still reads "the image remains to be decided", and not only "you cannot"):

    1. no image decided — the gate of RN-105, which holds in all THREE modes since RN-494; without artifact.project_image there is nothing to start;
    2. runner that never had a confirmed folder (null workspaceVerifiedAt, RN-423) — no local agent ever connected, so the action would fail for sure. The same honesty the Infra Lead's tool already practices when refusing LOCALLY before proposing (RN-508);
    3. role below maintainer — the minimum is that of the ENDPOINT (RN-102): both types require maintainer in decide.ts, and the comparison comes from roleAtLeast, never from a hand-written list of roles. What is taken away is the CONTROL, never the INFORMATION (ADR 0064): whoever cannot still sees state, image and resources, and the reason is said ONCE in TEXT — title on a disabled element does not open in Chromium.

    And what the screen does NOT know, it declares instead of promising. workspaceVerifiedAt is the record of ONE confirmation and never a heartbeat (RN-468): non-null does not prove a local agent connected NOW, and the api has no presence signal (what knows about now is the Phoenix channel, in the engine). So the runner row offers the button with a written caveat — "if it is not running now, the action fails when approved" — instead of a green dot that would lie.

    No ceiling moved. Every proposal on this screen is a proposed_action, always with a HUMAN clicking, never an agent; container_remove stays at the absolute ceiling (RN-418) and decide.ts stays byte for byte. The role read is the WORKSPACE one, and the gap is declared: the effective one is projectRole ?? workspaceRole (RN-471), and fetching project_members per row would be the network N+1 this page exists not to pay — whoever was DEMOTED in a project still sees the button and gets a 403, which is the repairable defect (it ends in a toast), not the invisible one.

    The repository is born at the handoff to the Dev Lead (RN-522)

    RN-522 — The repository is provisioned on ACCEPTING the Arquiteto → Dev Lead handoff, always local, and the failure never takes down the acceptance

    Revised by RN-582 (ADR 0165): the TRIGGER became accepting the handoff to the Arquiteto. Accepting to the Dev Lead described below keeps provisioning, as an idempotent second door, and the rest of this rule (always local, failure as an event, adopted is not a failure) still holds. The text below is that of the original decision.

    RN-541 took provisioning out of creation and declared that the trigger would come next. This is the trigger — and without it a created project would stay without a repository forever, because ProvisioningPage was the only caller of provisionRepository in the web and creation stopped navigating there.

    The moment is accepting the handoff from the Arquiteto to the Dev Lead, and not execution activation. They are DISTINCT instants, in this order: accepting the handoff activates the Dev Lead; activating execution is when the dev agents start claiming tasks. It is at the first that "development has started" becomes true, and it is what the product owner asked for — "quando o arquiteto passar o handoff para o desenvolvedor iniciar o desenvolvimento".

    The branch lives in AcceptHandoffUseCase, next to the 'infra' branch that already existed and for the same ordering reason: the effect happens before activateAgent, so that the agent wakes up in a project that already has somewhere to work.

    Always local. It is the only provider that asks for no credential at all — the if (providerName !== 'local') of ProvisionRepositoryUseCase never gets to resolve a secret, and LocalGitProvider.createRepo does not even read the accessToken the signature accepts. That is what makes automatic provisioning possible: nobody chose hosting in the middle of the acceptance, so there is no credential to fetch nor question to ask. Publishing to a remote provider remains a separate path (adoption, or conversion in Settings) — declared, not forgotten. Accepted side effect: protectBranch: false in the local provider makes the last bootstrap step degrade (step_degraded), never fail.

    The failure becomes an EVENT, never an exception. This use case has no transaction: when provisioning runs, updateStatus('accepted') and the handoff.accepted event are already COMMITTED. A throw would return a 500 to the user about a handoff that, in the database, was accepted — and would also prevent the activateAgent right below, leaving the Dev Lead not waking up because of a git failure. So the outcome goes to the event log as repository.provision_failed, with origem and the real message, and the acceptance proceeds. It is the usual rule: a failure records the origin and never becomes an empty response.

    What is NOT a failure: a project that ADOPTED a repository. ProvisionRepository refuses that case with ConflictException on purpose — bootstrapping a third-party repository only runs by plan approval (RN-045) —, but the project HAS a repository, so there is nothing to provision and recording that as a failure would lie about its state. The branch queries findByProjectId and exits before. A created repository that already exists is not skipped: it falls into the normal use case, which is idempotent by design ("running again does not fail"), and that is how an interrupted bootstrap completes.

    The MACHINE key the installer registers (RN-552)

    RN-552 — An internal route registers the MACHINE device key, for the installation's SOLE user, and registering REPLACES

    Session 7 of PHASE 30, closing point 4 of ADR 0155 on the kind of key ADR 0154 created. It is the gap RN-543 declared in writing and left open on purpose, by the DEPLOY_ENABLED rule: "no api route creates a machine key yet; that is install.sh, and it is born with the first caller". The caller arrived — it is session 6's installer —, so the route is born.

    The route. POST /internal/machine-device-keys, engine-service. Body { name, publicKeyJwk }, response 201 with { id, userId, name, createdAt, replacedKeyIds }. No GET and no DELETE.

    The credential is the SERVICE TOKEN, and the alternative was refused for a written reason. It is the same installer, in the same minute, in the step following that of RN-546: the BRABO_SERVICE_TOKEN was generated by install.sh itself and written to .env with mode 600, so presenting it proves control of the machine — which is exactly what this step wants to prove. The real candidate on the other side was the freshly created user's credential, and it contradicts ADR 0155 itself: the password is read in the TTY, "used and discarded", and point 5 declares that "the installer does not log in for anyone", which is why the first account's response does not return a session token. Requiring it here would force the installer to create, on the machine, the live session that ADR refused to create.

    What that choice costs, declared and not hidden. A leaked BRABO_SERVICE_TOKEN can now manufacture a durable access credential for a user — not only talk to the internal routes. It is stated here, in security-surface.md and in the controller's docblock, next to the sibling declaration of the first account. What the key grants did not increase: it gives the local agent exactly the projects its owner already reaches at developer, resolved against the requested project (RN-543).

    The route does not know how to choose whose key it is. There is no userId in the body. The owner is the installation's SOLE user, resolved by UserRepository.usuarioUnicoDaInstalacao() (LIMIT 2, never LIMIT 1: with one row it would be impossible to distinguish "there is exactly one" from "there are many"); with zero or more than one, 409 and nothing is written. It is the exact analogue of the condition of RN-546 — about the INSTALLATION, never about the requested argument —, and it is what prevents whoever has the token from choosing the victim. Declared consequence: in an installation with two people the route no longer works, for anyone. It goes silent as the first account one goes silent, and for the same reason — it belongs to the MOMENT of installation, not to the product's life.

    Registering REPLACES, never accumulates. Every active MACHINE key of the owner is revoked in the SAME transaction, and the ids come back in replacedKeyIds. A reinstalled machine is a legitimate case and keeps passing; a thousand machine keys become impossible — and not by a number that ages, but because the set of live machine keys of a user never exceeds one. The revocation comes BEFORE the registration: revoking afterwards would leave a window with both alive, and failing in the middle would leave the installation with two machine credentials and no way of knowing which is the new one. Only the MACHINE ones fall (project_id IS NULL): the PROJECT ones came from the browser (ADR 0118), in a flow this route does not know, and taking them down would erase the pairing of whoever already uses the product — the error RN-545 named when refusing to convert someone else's installation silently.

    The response returns the id because it becomes the kid. It is the lesson of RN-475, the most expensive in this area: the record's id is written INSIDE the private JWK, in the kid, and the whole chain only PASSES IT ON — the local agent reads jwk.kid, the ticket JWT carries it in the header, PatAuthGuard finds the public key by it. Nobody derives that id from anything else, and it was for lacking it that the browser's automatic mode never authenticated. The userId also comes back, RESOLVED by the api: the caller does not send it, and returning it lets the installer check against the account it just created instead of assuming.

    The private key never travels, and one that arrives is REFUSED. The pair is generated on the machine and only the public half goes up — the same design as the browser, for the same reason, keeping true the sentence RN-519 uses. The shape validation became a SINGLE rule in the domain (exigirJwkPublicaEd25519), called by the TWO registrars: two copies would diverge on the first day one of them changed, as the password policy of RN-546 already resolves. And it gained a case neither of the two had: a JWK with d answers 400 saying what arrived. d is the private half of an OKP JWK (RFC 8037 §2) and only arrives by the mistake of whoever serialized the whole pair — before, it passed the check (it has kty, crv and x like any public one) and was written. Refusing is the answer; the message names what came, because a generic "invalid JWK" would make the person try again with the same file.

    Its own kind in the auth trail. machine_device_key_registered: this is the only durable credential of a user that is born without that user authenticating anything — what proves is control of the machine. Under suspicion of a service token leak, it is that row that says when and for whom it was created, and the metadata carries the ids it replaced, never the JWK nor the name.

    No GET and no DELETE, and what that costs. Listing through here would publish, to whoever only has the machine's token, the credentials inventory of a person; revoking already exists where there is a human owner (DELETE /projects/:projectId/runner-device-keys/:deviceKeyId, which matches by {id, usuário} and never by project). The asymmetry has a price, and it is declared: in an installation that has no project yet, no screen reaches a machine key — and that is precisely why registering REPLACES instead of leaving orphans behind, which would be alive and unreachable.

    What did NOT come in: a public route (same race as RN-546); userId in the body; a machine key for an installation with a team (declared above as a gap, not as an accident); a new table (a machine key is still a row of runner_device_keys with project_id NULL, ADR 0154 point 1) — and no migration, because the column is already nullable since RN-543.

    The self-demotion ceiling also on REMOVAL (RN-556)

    RN-556 — Removing one's own project_members row is refused with 403 when the net effect is a demotion

    About the number. The jump from RN-542 to 556 is deliberate: the range 543–555 is reserved for PHASE 30, which has already allocated it in branches in flight. Allocating here would produce the collision this repository has already observed three times at the same instant (ADR 0148 ×2, RN-522 ×2, RN-523 ×2), resolved afterwards by DATE. Nothing was skipped by mistake.

    ADR 0127 put the two ceilings of RN-472 only on the WRITE path and declared the third movement open, in writing and with the estimated cost: "RemoveProjectMemberUseCase did NOT gain a ceiling… The premise that 'removal is always benign' is false, and it stays written here so as not to be rediscovered". This RN closes that door — it is BRB-001, security P1.

    Removing does not erase a role, it SWAPS the effective role. ResolveEffectiveRoleUseCase.forProject is projectRole ?? workspaceRole (RN-471), and the overlay holds in BOTH directions. Remove the project row, and the effective one starts resolving by the second term — which can be SMALLER. A maintainer whose authority came from the project row, viewer in the workspace, removed their own row and fell to viewer with no way back through the screen: restoring is POST :projectId/members, which requires the just-abandoned maintainer. Without any workspace role, the fall is to NO access.

    It is ceiling 2, not a new ceiling. ehAutoRebaixamento compares TODAY's effective role with the AFTER one, and never needed to know by which route the second arrived: in add the after-role comes from the body, in removal it comes from the workspace. remocaoEhAutoRebaixamento is that application, and it DELEGATES — it reimplements no comparison at all. It exists as its own function for ONE case the other's signature cannot state: an actor without a workspace role, where the after-role is "none", which is not a Role. That case is the maximum demotion and refuses.

    movement outcome
    removing one's own row, workspace with the SAME role passes — it is how someone leaves the list
    removing one's own row, workspace with a LOWER role 403
    removing one's own row, WITHOUT a workspace role 403 — the fall is to no access
    removing ANOTHER person's row, even if they fall passes — the usual legitimate capability
    removing the row that restricted the WORKSPACE owner passes — it can only RAISE

    Ceiling 1 gains no counterpart, and the absence is a decision. owner is the top of ROLE_ORDER: removing the project row of someone who is owner in the workspace can only raise their effective role, or keep it. More than harmless, it is the ONLY way to undo a restriction ceiling 1 prevents from being created. A ceiling there would refuse only benign movements and make permanent the state ADR 0127 was born to eliminate. It is written next to the function and pinned in a test.

    Without a threshold, like ceiling 2 — and the price comes with it. The refusal is "oneself", not "below maintainer", for the same reason as RN-472: a threshold would copy a number from the controller's @RequireRole into the domain and would age silently if the route changed its minimum. The declared price is the self-removal of whoever has owner in the project and maintainer in the workspace: reversible, and refused too. It was the only benign movement that passed before and now refuses; it stays reachable by another maintainer.

    The message is its OWN. Whoever clicked "remove" did not ask to change any role, so MENSAGEM_TETO_AUTO_REBAIXAMENTO_POR_REMOCAO states the MECHANISM — without the project row the role falls to the workspace's, and coming back requires the abandoned role — instead of reusing the add sentence, which would talk about a movement the person did not make.

    The screen does not change, and the refusal shows up. MembersSection.handleRemove already shows mensagemDaApi(erro, …) in a toast (RN-471), so the api's sentence arrives without a line of web. Unlike ceiling 1, this gate IS computable on the client — but computing only it would produce the half-gate ADR 0127 refused.

    Master key rotation stops being trial and error (RN-562, RN-563)

    RN-562 — Master key rotation is proven end to end, in both tables

    The procedure with the worst outcome in the Runbook now has a NAMED verification: a test walks through the whole rotation — encrypt with K1, publish K2, rewrap, discard K1 and still decrypt — against user_credentials and project_git_connections, with a real Postgres.

    Why integration, and not one more unit case. What already existed (envelope-encryption.service.spec.ts, the rotação da chave mestra describe) exercises encrypt/decrypt/rewrap in memory, and that does not prove the only thing step 3 of the runbook depends on: that the script walks through both tables. Converting half the holdings and reporting success, discarding the old key would make the other half unreadable forever. The proof of that is the assertion about the two rows — and it fails when the script's list of tables shrinks.

    Idempotency goes into the same test, because it is the property the runbook promises to whoever interrupts the script: the second round reports re-embrulhados=0 and já na chave atual=1 in both tables.

    An unreadable row does not abort the others. A record wrapped by a THIRD key — the case the runbook calls "came from another environment" — is counted, identified by table and id, and lets the others continue; its envelope stays untouched.

    What the test required of the code: rewrap-deks.ts was a main() fired at MODULE LOAD, so importing it from a spec would run the rotation. The core became reenvelopar(db, cofre, reportarFalha), exported, and main() — which reads the environment, opens the pool, prints and chooses the exit code — now runs only under require.main === module. The script's name and the runbook's invocation (node scripts/rewrap-deks.js) did NOT change.

    No key and no secret is literal in the test: both are born from randomBytes each round. A constant passphrase in a fixture is a string that looks like a secret going into history, and gitleaks sweeps branches.

    RN-563 — The envelope says which key wrapped it, and that label never decides whether it opens

    user_credentials and project_git_connections gain a nullable key_id text — the fingerprint of the master key that wrapped that DEK. With it, the question that decides step 3 of the rotation ("is there still a credential on the old key?") becomes a query:

    select count(*) from user_credentials      where key_id is distinct from '<atual>'
union all
select count(*) from project_git_connections where key_id is distinct from '<atual>';

    IS DISTINCT FROM, and never <>: with <>, the row with a NULL key_id — the holdings prior to this column — would disappear from the count, and "I don't know which key" would become "it is already on the current one", which is the reading that makes someone discard the old key too early.

    The value is HMAC-SHA256(chave derivada, 'brabo-master-key-id') truncated to 8 bytes, and not a counter in .env nor a hash of the passphrase. There is no new oracle, and that was MEASURED, not assumed: whoever reads the database already has a perfect verification oracle — the envelope itself is AES-256-GCM, which authenticates, so testing a candidate passphrase already cost one scrypt and one decipher. Testing it against the fingerprint costs the SAME scrypt. And there is no new variable for the operator to get wrong: the value is a pure function of the key they already published.

    The label is OBSERVABILITY, never AUTHORITY. decrypt stays byte for byte as it was — tries the current one, falls back to the previous one, GCM decides — and rewrap keeps deciding "it is already on the current key" by ATTEMPT. Trusting the label would make a row that LIES (label "current", envelope on the old key) be skipped silently, stay out of the re-wrapped count, and step 3 would make it unreadable forever. Incoherent metadata becomes secret loss; that is why the test that pins this rule is that of a lying row being re-wrapped anyway.

    What the label buys on failure: when NEITHER of the two keys opens, the message stops being generic and names the case — "came from another environment" (unknown label), "incoherent label or tampered record" (label says current and does not open) and "has no key_id" (row prior to this column) are different diagnoses with different actions. None of these messages carries the passphrase, derived key or secret content — only fingerprints.

    No migration of the holdings. The key_id is born at the next write (encrypt and rewrap write it). Today's rows stay NULL, and in an existing installation the query only becomes valid after the first rotation. Forcing a rewrap of everything just to fill the column would turn observability into a risky operation on all credentials.

    The operator needs the current fingerprint, otherwise the column compares against nothing: the api records it at boot in one line, and the rotation warning that already existed now names BOTH.

    RN-567 — proposed_action.created says WHICH rule decided: the reason of decide() now survives when the action passes

    decide() always returned a pair — policy and reason —, and the reason is written at every return point: insufficient IAM, the container floor (RN-492), agent_autonomy, the lines of permissions.json, the compound command, and each absolute ceiling. But ProposeActionUseCase only kept it in one place: rejectionReason, which initialStatusFor fills in only when the policy denies. On an auto-approval — the outcome that most needs auditing — the event log said "the policy decided" (RN-049) and never which rule. status made auto-approval distinguishable from a click; the reason is the next step.

    The rule: the payload of the SESSION event proposed_action.created gains reason, with the string from decide() as is, in all THREE outcomes — auto_approved, pending and denied. No second "structured" rule is born: the string is already the source, and a parallel enum would diverge from it on the first new ceiling. In denied the value is the SAME that becomes rejectionReason.

    The outbox does NOT gain the field, and that is a decision. The outbox row proposed_action.created is an api↔engine contract, and no engine consumer reads the reason; widening a contract without a consumer is the cut that ADR 0153 names. The session_event.appended row that AppendSessionEventUseCase writes for the same event carries only eventId/seq/type, so the reason also does not leak through it.

    Absent is not "no reason". An event written before this rule does not have the field, and there is no reprocessing nor new column: whoever reads treats an absent reason as "not recorded". Every new event has the field, because Decision.reason is a mandatory string in the type.

    Nothing in decide() changes — no ceiling, no verdict, no string. The screen also does not change in this rule: the reason comes to EXIST in the log, and showing it is another delivery. (Since RN-614 the screen shows it on the event's line in the log panel and in the ApprovalCard, through the same sentence.)

    What the reason does NOT say, declared: it names the rule, not the scope's ROOT — point 7 of ADR 0055 asked for which root authorized, and escopo: cd dentro da pasta do projeto does not carry the path. (The root started going in the event in its OWN field since RN-609, relative and never absolute.) In the compound command, the reason says all segments hit allow, without saying which pattern matched which segment. And the lines of permissions.json repeat the command's TOKENS in the text (the label of matchAgainstFile) — the same command that already lives in proposed_actions.payload and on the approval card.

    RN-569 — The graph is rebuilt from the event log by the SAME translator as the live projector, without touching the outbox, and never comes out as a silent success

    ADR 0152 (decision 4) refused a backup of neo4j_data based on a premise — the graph can be discarded because it can be rebuilt — whose mechanism did not exist: grep for reprojet/reproject in apps/ and scripts/ came back empty, and application/graph-projection/ only had the FORWARD projector. While it did not exist, the graph was not discardable: it was lost.

    The rule: apps/api/src/scripts/reprojetar-grafo.ts (pnpm --filter api grafo:reprojetar; node scripts/reprojetar-grafo.js in the image) rebuilds the graph by sweeping the source. Five decisions, each with a reason:

    1. A single translator. The event → node/edge translation LEFT GraphProjector for GraphEventTranslator, and both paths call it — the projector reaches the source through an outbox row, the reprojection through a cursor. Two translators would diverge, and the divergent one would be the one that runs once a year. The projector's injection surface did NOT change (it builds the translator with the dependencies it already received). A test fails a new type in GRAPH_PROJECTABLE_EVENT_TYPES without a translation.
    2. The sources are two, and they are the real ones. handoff.offered, psychologist.hypothesis_proposed and anamnese.profile_updated come from session_events; the Interacao comes from sessions in closed/closed_abnormally, because closing a session is a pure transition and leaves no event in the log. PromptTemplate/PromptVersion do NOT come from the event log and are NOT reprojected — they come back through scripts/dev/seed-prompts.ts.
    3. Idempotent, in batches, and never deletes. Every write is a MERGE on a natural key; running again is the way to resume. session_events is swept in id order (ULID, the primary key), 200 per batch, and --after-event resumes after the printed cursor. With --project, only that project's sessions.
    4. It does not touch the outbox. The live projector keeps its progress in outbox_events.processed_at; the reprojection neither reads nor writes that table, and that is why it runs with the api up without stealing, reopening or marking rows.
    5. Never a silent success. A disabled graph is refused BEFORE reading the log (an empty scope "would pass" with zero projected); a Neo4j that drops midway stops with the last completed event; a nonexistent project is refused without writing anything; and an item with an incoherent payload is counted, named, and the process exits with 1.

    What this rule does NOT close: PerfilAnamnese is a snapshot per user + dimension, WITHOUT a project — the last to write wins —, so a round with --project may leave it at that project's value when another wrote later; the full round restores the global last one. There is no time measurement on a large event log (the only real round was the dev compose, 98 events, 2.5 s), and the proof on the local cluster that BRB-018 asks for was not done — it remains open.

    RN-573 — The creation wizard only preselects the mode the installation executes: without a broker, runner is the suggested one and container/mounted stay inert with the reason in text

    In a real installation of v6.1.0 (AT-085), the wizard preselected mounted — install.sh always writes BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE, and with a known base RN-513 preselected the mode. But the installation by Release has no container broker (the image is not published, decision 7 of ADR 0150), and container/mounted only start a container through the broker (RN-503). Result: six dev.blocked_by_container and two container.start_failed — nobody works on the project, forever (RN-502).

    The rule (ADR 0161):

    1. The api says whether there is a broker, on the route the wizard already reads. GET workspaces/:workspaceId/projects-base now returns brokerConfigurado next to projectsBase — the same question ("what mode does this INSTALLATION execute?"), the same minimum (maintainer), no new route. The source is ContainerBrokerPort.configurado(), the same as the read of the observed state. It says BROKER_URL exists, never that the broker answers.
    2. Three states, which do not collapse. Broker confirmed: RN-513 intact. Confirmed absence: container and mounted stay on the screen, inert (the control leaves, the information stays — RN-102), the reason is stated ONCE in text below the cards, and runner is the preselected one. I don't know (loading, failing query, absent field): does not become "it has" — mounted is NOT preselected, the revision of RN-513 — and also does not become "it doesn't have": no card locks and nothing is asserted in text; container stays selected, as before.
    3. The human choice does not point to what does not run. Whoever clicked a mode before the answer arrived, and the answer confirms it does not execute here, falls to runner — the same rule that already knocked mounted down when the base disappears.

    What this rule does NOT close: the mode conversion (RN-559) still offers container/mounted in an installation without a broker; the installer does not ask whether to turn the broker on, because its image cannot be obtained by a Release installation (measured — see ADR 0161); and in the development compose, which brings up the broker by default (RN-512) but leaves BROKER_URL empty until someone puts it in .env, the warning shows up — and it is right, because without the variable the api never calls the broker.
